description: Evernote is a popular note-taking and organization app. While it has a free tier, it is heavily limited (2 devices, 60MB upload/month, no offline access). Paid plans start at $10.83/month (Personal) and $14.99/month (Professional), which many users find expensive for a note-taking app.
painPoints: Free plan limited to 2 devices and 60MB monthly upload — very restrictive
Personal plan at $10.83/month is expensive for a note-taking app
Professional at $14.99/month adds AI features but still feels overpriced
Offline access is paid-only (even on mobile)
Sync speed can be slow, especially on free tier
Data lock-in — exporting notes is clunky (ENEX format)
whySwitch: Get unlimited notes for free (no 50-note limit)
Get native Linux support with open-source alternatives
Own your data — use local-first alternatives
Avoid vendor lock-in — export is easy with alternatives

alternatives.name: Obsidian
alternatives.pricing: Free for personal use; Sync $10/month; Publish $20/month
features: Local-first: notes stored as Markdown files on your device
Graph view to visualize note connections
Mobile apps with sync (paid) or via iCloud/Dropbox (free)
pros: Notes are plain Markdown files — you own them forever
Free for personal use (no monthly upload limits like Evernote free)
Bi-directional linking is powerful for building a knowledge base
Plugin ecosystem is incredible (kanban, calendaring, etc.)
Local-first means fast and works offline natively
cons: Sync between devices requires either manual setup (iCloud/Dropbox) or paid Obsidian Sync
Learning curve for new users (Markdown, plugins, settings)
Mobile apps are less polished than Evernote's
No collaboration features (not a team wiki)
alternatives.bestFor: Personal knowledge management, researchers, and people who want future-proof Markdown notes
alternatives.reason: Free to use, Obsidian offers a cost-effective alternative to Evernote.

alternatives.name: Joplin
alternatives.pricing: 100% free and open-source; optional End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) add-on $
features: Sync via Dropbox, OneDrive, Nextcloud, or WebDAV
pros: Completely free with no feature gating
Syncs via your own cloud (Dropbox, OneDrive, etc.)
Good Evernote import (preserves notebooks and tags)
cons: UI is functional but not as polished as Evernote or Notion
Sync setup requires connecting to cloud storage (slight technical step)
No collaboration features (single-user focused)
Web Clipper is less powerful than Evernote's
alternatives.bestFor: Privacy-conscious users who want a free, open-source Evernote alternative
alternatives.reason: 100% free and open-source Joplin is a compelling alternative to Evernote.

alternatives.pricing: Free for personal use; Plus $10/month; Business $18/month
features: All-in-one workspace: notes, databases, wikis, project management

Combines notes with databases — much more powerful than Evernote
Real-time collaboration built-in (great for shared knowledge bases)
cons: Learning curve — the block-based system is different from traditional note apps
Can get slow with very large workspaces
Offline support is weaker than Obsidian or Joplin
Free tier has file upload limits (5MB per file)
alternatives.bestFor: Teams, project managers, and people who want notes + databases + wikis in one tool
alternatives.reason: Free to use, Notion (free tier) offers a cost-effective alternative to Evernote.

No folders or notebooks (only tags)

alternatives.bestFor: People who want the simplest possible note-taking experience
alternatives.reason: 100% free and open-source Simplenote is a compelling alternative to Evernote.

alternatives.name: Microsoft OneNote
alternatives.pricing: Free (included with Microsoft account); desktop version free with Windows
features: Free-form canvas (type anywhere, not just top-to-bottom)
pros: Completely free — no paid tier at all (unlike Evernote)
Free-form canvas is unique — great for visual notes and diagrams
Excellent handwriting and drawing support (great for tablet users)
Deep integration with Microsoft Office ecosystem

migrationGuide.overview: Migrating from Evernote is well-supported. Evernote allows exporting notebooks as .enex files, which can be imported into Joplin, Obsidian (via plugin), and Notion. The key is preserving your notebook structure and tags.
steps: In Evernote, select notebooks → Export → ENEX format (with tags and attachments)
For Joplin: File → Import → Evernote (.enex) — preserves notebooks and tags
For Obsidian: install 'Evernote Converter' plugin or import via Joplin as intermediate
For Notion: use the Evernote importer in Notion (Settings → Import)
Re-create your tag structure and notebook links in the new tool
Cancel Evernote subscription after confirming all notes are accessible
tips: Joplin's Evernote import is the most reliable — if other tools fail, import to Joplin first, then export to Markdown for Obsidian
If you relied on Evernote's Web Clipper, Notion's Web Clipper is the closest replacement
Obsidian's Markdown files are future-proof — even if Obsidian dies, your notes are readable in any text editor
OneNote is the best free alternative if you're already in the Microsoft ecosystem — it's completely free with no device limits

faq.q: Will I lose my notes if I cancel Evernote?
faq.a: No — Evernote allows you to export your notes as .enex files before canceling. Even after canceling, you can still access your notes in read-only mode on the devices you've synced. However, you should export your notes as a backup before canceling.

faq.q: What about Evernote's PDF annotation and document search?
faq.a: Obsidian with the 'Annotater' plugin, or Notion (with its PDF viewer), can handle PDF annotation. For document search within images (OCR), OneNote has excellent OCR built-in. Most alternatives handle PDFs well, though the workflow may be slightly different.

faq.q: Is there a tool that works exactly like Evernote?
faq.a: Microsoft OneNote is the closest in terms of free-form note-taking and visual notes. Joplin is the closest in terms of notebook/tag structure. However, most modern alternatives (Obsidian, Notion) are actually more powerful than Evernote — they just have a different workflow.

While OneNote itself is free, it's often compared against paid note-taking apps.

No Markdown support (uses rich text only)
Integration is deep with Microsoft Office, but weak for non-Microsoft users

Apple Notes is excellent for Apple users. For structured note-taking (outline-style), Logseq or Roam Research are better choices.

migrationGuide.overview: OneNote notes can be exported as .onepkg files, but most alternatives don't import this format directly. The best approach is to export your OneNote notebooks as PDF or use OneNote's 'Copy Text from Picture' and manual copying for smaller note collections.
steps: For small note collections: manually copy-paste or use OneNote's export to PDF, then re-create in the new tool
For large collections: use OneNote's 'Export → PDF' for each section, then use the PDFs as reference while re-creating in Markdown in Obsidian
For structured migration: export OneNote pages as .mht (web archive), then convert to Markdown using Pandoc
Set up your new tool's folder/notebook structure to match your OneNote organization
Use Obsidian's 'Daily Notes' or Logseq's 'Journals' if you used OneNote for daily notes
tips: If you have many notes, prioritize migrating your most-used notebooks first — you can keep OneNote installed as read-only for the rest
Obsidian's 'Tags' pane is a good replacement for OneNote's tag search
For handwritten notes in OneNote: export as images, then use Obsidian or Notion to embed them
Notion's 'Import from Evernote' won't help with OneNote, but you can share OneNote pages to Notion via 'Copy Link' and embed as web pages

faq.q: Can I export my OneNote notes to use in other apps?
faq.a: OneNote allows exporting notebooks as .onepkg (OneNote format), .pdf, or .mht (web archive). For migrating to Markdown-based tools (Obsidian, Logseq), export to .mht and use Pandoc to convert to Markdown. For small collections, manual copy-paste is often the simplest path.

faq.q: What if I only use OneNote for handwritten notes on my iPad?
faq.a: If you use OneNote primarily for handwriting, consider Apple Notes (if on iPad), GoodNotes (one-time purchase, excellent for handwriting), or Notability. These are much better for handwriting and PDF annotation than OneNote.

faq.q: Is there a free alternative with handwriting support like OneNote?
faq.a: Apple Notes (free, excellent handwriting) and Google Keep (free, simpler) both support handwriting on mobile. For advanced handwriting and PDF annotation, GoodNotes ($9.99 one-time) or Notability (subscription or one-time) are the best iPad alternatives to OneNote's handwriting features.

description: Cubase is a professional Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) developed by Steinberg. It is widely used in music production, film scoring, and game audio. Pricing starts at $99.99 (Elements) and goes up to $579.99 (Pro), which is a significant investment for hobbyist musicians.
painPoints: Expensive: $99.99 (Elements) to $579.99 (Pro) — steep for beginners
Steinberg's licensing system (Steinberg Licenser) is clunky and hardware-dongle-based for some versions
Resource-heavy — requires a powerful computer for large projects
Steep learning curve for beginners
No native Linux version
whySwitch: Excellent free and cheaper DAWs exist. Reaper is only $60 (discounted) and is incredibly powerful. Audacity (free, open-source) is great for simple recording and editing. LMMS (free, open-source) is good for beat-making and electronic music. Cakewalk by BandLab is a full-featured DAW that is now completely free. For many producers, these alternatives cover 90% of what they need.

migrationGuide.overview: Migrating from Cubase to another DAW involves re-creating your projects in the new tool. There's no direct project file conversion. The best approach is to export your Cubase tracks as audio (WAV/FLAC) and import them into the new DAW, then re-add MIDI data and effects.
steps: Export each Cubase track as a separate WAV/FLAC audio file (with effects baked in or not, depending on your needs)
If you have MIDI tracks, export the MIDI data as .mid files and import into the new DAW
Set up your new DAW's project structure (tracks, routing, groups)
Import the audio files and MIDI files into the new DAW
Re-create any Cubase-specific effects or processing using the new DAW's built-in effects or third-party VSTs
For future projects, start working directly in the new DAW
tips: Reaper's $60 license is the best value in DAWs — even if you keep Cubase for some projects, Reaper is worth having as a backup
If you use Cubase primarily for MIDI composition, Reaper and Bitwig both have excellent MIDI editors
Cakewalk is the best free alternative if you're on Windows — it was a premium DAW (Sonar) that is now completely free
LMMS is great for beat-making and electronic music, but it's not a full replacement for Cubase's recording and mixing capabilities

faq.q: Can I open my Cubase project files (.cpr) in other DAWs?
faq.a: No — there's no direct project file conversion between DAWs. You need to export your Cubase tracks as audio (WAV) and MIDI, then import them into the new DAW. Some third-party tools claim to convert project files, but they're unreliable. The cleanest approach is audio/MIDI export.

faq.q: What if I have third-party VST plugins I bought for Cubase?
faq.a: VST plugins are generally compatible across all DAWs that support VST. Reaper, Cakewalk, Bitwig, and LMMS (on Windows) all support VST plugins. Your plugin licenses are separate from Cubase — you can use them in any compatible DAW.

faq.q: Is there a free DAW that's as powerful as Cubase?
faq.a: Cakewalk by BandLab is the closest — it was a premium DAW (Sonar Platinum, $500+) that is now completely free. It has advanced MIDI editing, mixing, and scoring features. For electronic music, LMMS is free and capable. For overall value, Reaper ($60) is arguably more powerful than Cubase for most use cases.

description: Ableton Live is a popular DAW known for its unique Session View (clip launcher) and excellent live performance capabilities. Pricing starts at $99 (Intro), $449 (Standard), and $749 (Suite). The high price of Standard and Suite puts it out of reach for many bedroom producers.
painPoints: Expensive: $449 (Standard), $749 (Suite) — significant investment
Intro ($99) is too limited (16 audio tracks, 16 MIDI tracks) for serious production
No notation view (score editor) — unlike Cubase, Logic Pro, or Musescore
Resource-heavy — Session View with many clips can tax older computers

whySwitch: Bitwig Studio ($399) offers a similar clip-launching workflow and is cheaper than Ableton Standard. Reaper ($60) is incredibly powerful and lightweight. For live performance specifically, there's also Maschine+ (hardware) or even a simple setup with a launchpad and free software. Many producers find that Bitwig or Reaper covers 90% of what they use Ableton for.

migrationGuide.overview: Like Cubase, Ableton Live project files (.als) can't be opened in other DAWs. You need to export your tracks as audio (WAV/FLAC) and MIDI, then import into the new DAW. For clip-launching workflows, Bitwig is the closest alternative.
steps: Open your Ableton project and export each track as WAV/FLAC (with or without effects, depending on your needs)
Export MIDI clips as .mid files
Set up your new DAW (Bitwig is closest for clip launching; Reaper for traditional production)
Import audio and MIDI files into the new DAW
Re-create Ableton-specific effects using the new DAW's built-in effects or VSTs
For future projects, start working directly in the new DAW
tips: Bitwig Studio is the closest alternative to Ableton's clip-launching workflow — if you love Session View, try Bitwig first
Reaper is incredible value at $60 — even if you keep Ableton for live performance, Reaper is worth having for production
If you use Ableton primarily for live performance with a clip launcher, consider adding a hardware clip launcher (like Novation Launchpad) and using free software like QMidiLab for Linux
Cakewalk is free and full-featured — if you're on Windows and don't need clip launching, it's an excellent alternative

faq.q: Can I open my Ableton project files (.als) in other DAWs?
faq.a: No — there's no direct project file conversion. You need to export your Ableton tracks as audio (WAV) and MIDI, then import them into the new DAW. Bitwig can import some Ableton clip arrangements, but it's not seamless.

faq.q: What about my Ableton packs and instruments (Wavetable, Operator, etc.)?
faq.a: Ableton's built-in instruments and packs are exclusive to Ableton. You'll need to find alternatives (VST plugins) for those sounds. Bitwig has its own built-in instruments (POLYSYNTH, THE GRID) that can replace some Ableton instruments. For free alternatives, check out the built-in instruments in LMMS or free VSTs from Spitfire LABS, Vital, etc.

faq.q: Is there a free DAW with a clip launcher like Ableton?
faq.a: No free DAW has a clip launcher exactly like Ableton's Session View. Bitwig ($399) is the closest. For live performance on a budget, consider using a hardware clip launcher (Novation Launchpad) with free software, or use Ableton Live Intro ($99) which includes Session View with limitations.

Perpetual license option is very expensive ($599 for Pro Tools Studio perpetual)
Resource-heavy — requires powerful hardware and often an Avid audio interface for low latency
Steep learning curve, especially for those used to other DAWs
No MIDI notation view (score editor) in many versions
Collaboration (Pro Tools Clud) requires additional subscription
whySwitch: Pro Tools is industry-standard for a reason, but for home studios and indie producers, it's overkill. Reaper ($60) is incredibly powerful and lightweight. Cubase (one-time purchase) and Logic Pro ($199 one-time, macOS only) are both excellent. For film scoring specifically, Cubase and Logic Pro have better scoring features than Pro Tools. Unless you're working in a professional studio that requires Pro Tools, you can switch to a cheaper or one-time-purchase DAW.

migrationGuide.overview: Pro Tools project files (.ptx) can't be opened in other DAWs. You need to export your Pro Tools tracks as audio (WAV/FLAC at the desired sample rate/depth) and import them into the new DAW. For MIDI data, export as .mid files. The hardest part is re-creating Pro Tools-specific effects and routing.
steps: Open your Pro Tools session and export each track as WAV/FLAC (bounce to disk)
If you have MIDI tracks, export as .mid files
Set up your new DAW (Reaper, Logic Pro, Cubase, or Studio One)
Import audio and MIDI files into the new DAW
Re-create Pro Tools-specific effects using the new DAW's built-in effects or third-party AAX/VST/AU plugins
For future projects, start working directly in the new DAW
tips: Reaper's $60 license is the best value — even if you occasionally need Pro Tools for collaboration, Reaper can handle 99% of production tasks
Logic Pro ($199 one-time) is the best value for macOS users — it includes everything (no tiers, no subscriptions)
If you collaborate with studios that use Pro Tools, consider keeping a subscription for those specific projects — use Reaper or Logic for everything else
Pro Tools' AAX plugin format is proprietary — if you own AAX plugins, they won't work in other DAWs. Look for VST/AU versions of those plugins

faq.q: Can I open my Pro Tools project files (.ptx) in other DAWs?
faq.a: No — there's no direct project file conversion. You need to export your Pro Tools tracks as audio (WAV) and MIDI, then import them into the new DAW. Some third-party tools claim to convert, but they're unreliable.

faq.q: What if I need to collaborate with studios that use Pro Tools?
faq.a: You have three options: (1) Keep a Pro Tools subscription for those specific collaborations, (2) Export your tracks as audio stems and send them to the studio (they can import into their Pro Tools session), or (3) Use Reaper or Logic Pro for your work and only use Pro Tools at the studio.

faq.q: Is Pro Tools really necessary for professional work?
faq.a: It depends. Pro Tools is the industry standard in major recording studios and post-production houses. If you're working in those environments, you need Pro Tools. For home studios, indie production, and even many professional film/game scoring projects, other DAWs (Reaper, Logic Pro, Cubase) are perfectly acceptable and often preferred for their workflow advantages.
